*Anuttaraprakāśapañcāśikā* by Ādyanātha, from the Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies (KSTS), Volume 14 — Containing the *Bhāvopahāra* of Cakrapāṇinātha with the commentary (*Ṭīkā*) of Ramyadevabhaṭṭa — Following the *Bhāvopahāra* and *Bodhapañcadaśikā*.
Author: Ādyanātha
Editor: Śāstrī, Mukundarāma Description: The *Anuttaraprakāśapañcāśikā* by Ādyanātha, from the KSTS series, volume 14, following the *Bhāvopahāra* and *Bodhapañcadaśikā*.
Notes: This electronic text was data-entered by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Mark Dyczkowski. Revision 0: October 18, 2007.
Publisher: Research Department, Jammu and Kashmir State Publication Year: 1918 Publication City: Bombay
Country of Publication: India Composed by Śrī Ādinātha:
[To him who is the ground of rest, distinct from the various streams of all consciousness...]
Homage to Śiva, the ocean of consciousness whose body is the subject!

Śiva is a single mass of light consisting of the uncreated reflective awareness of "I," [united] with his own power, which is non-different from his own self and whose nature is reflective awareness. (1)
Manifesting the entire universe from Śiva down to the earth as his own body,
the Lord, who delights in the great drama of the five-fold cosmic acts, sports.
Nor is there even a discourse on the selflessness of the universe and its power, for they possess bodies that are the universe itself;
nor is there any real distinction between the universe and those whose very form is the universe. (3)
If there were a difference [between the Self and the world], how could the world exist as distinct from existence (sattā) and manifestation (sphurattā)?
If it is argued that the appearance of existence therein arises from its connection with existence and manifestation, [then the following applies].

What [connection] could there be between the non-existent and the existent? Yet this very connection is asserted by you. Indeed, a connection is easily obtained only through the acquisition of its own nature; for there can be no connection for that which lacks reality.
Having no established relationship with those two, it does not depend on anything;
if there were dependence, this [entity] would have no stability whatsoever.
By its very nature, radiance and existence are not subject to destruction;
if destruction were not admitted, even insentience would be excluded.
Therefore, since there is no other possible state of being, consciousness alone remains;
consequently, the identity of the world with consciousness, which was the subject under discussion, is not subverted. (8)
Who can limit the power of Śambhu, who transcends the universe, whose manifestation as something other than light is solely the outpouring of his own sovereignty? (9)
Everything is of the nature of self-luminosity, though it has reached a state of pure darkness;
whatever exists in this world does not transcend luminosity.
"This has reached the path of discernment"—this is the ultimate reality;
the intellect of those whose minds are one-pointedly attentive is the witness here. (11)
Of what use are those wretched means of valid cognition, whose very selves are animated by consciousness?
For the solar light does not depend upon the illumination of a lamp.
Let this principle of consciousness (dhītattva), purified by the descent of power (śaktipāta), be examined;
for indeed, everything is reflected within it, like in a mirror of vast and stainless expanse. 13.
Thus, everything consists of consciousness and is sealed by the thirty-six divisions;
first is the pure principle (tattva), which is fivefold and beyond darkness (tamas).
Śiva, Śakti, Sadākhya, Īśa, and Vidya—thus [the system] is divided;
yet it was determined by Śiva that its essence consists of the phonemes from 'a' (akṣa) up to 'kṣa' (śānta). 15.
Kalā, vidyā, rāga, kāla, and niyati are said to be bondage;
they consist of the letters beginning with 'va' and ending with 'ya', preceded by Māyā. (16)

The Puruṣa, Śakti, mind, intellect, ego, and the five [tanmātras] beginning with sound; the five [organs] beginning with hearing, the [channels] beginning with nāḍī and ṇāḍī, and the five [organs] beginning with speech. || 17 ||

The five subtle elements beginning with *ña* and the five [gross elements] beginning with *ṅa*, such as space and so forth, are known as the Śiva-tattva of the Lord, which is the first vibration of Him desiring to emit [the universe]. (18)
His very will, when it has faded away, is known as the principle of power (śaktitattva);
by his own will, he creates the universe and remains there, concealing it with the sense of "I-ness" (ahantā).
That very reality is Sādākhya, intent upon bestowing grace upon all;
that indeed is the Īśvara-tattva, perceiving this entire universe as "this-ness" (idantayā). 20.
The cognition of the identity between "I" and "this" is called *vidyā*; the notion of difference regarding objects that are like one's own limbs is the *māyātattva*. (21)
Śiva, when contracted by the grasp of Māyā, is called the principle of the individual soul (puṃstattva).
He alone is indeed designated as the transmigrating being, the living soul, and the enjoyer. (22)

The powers of knowledge, agency, fullness, eternity, and so forth, become contracted through that limitation; they are considered to consist of the *kalās* and other [categories] due to this contraction. (23)
From the illusory self (māyātman) arises that which is called *kalā*, the cause of limited agency;
*vidyā* is the cause of limited knowledge; and *rāga* is the cause of attachment. (24)
Time is that which effects limitation; destiny is the fixed order that "this alone is for me to do, and nothing else"—it takes the form of a constraint. (25)
Prakṛti is the equilibrium of the guṇas and the birthplace of the ego (ahaṅkāra) and other evolutes;
the ego (ahaṅkṛti) is the cause of the intellect that conceives "I" and "this is mine."
Intellect (buddhi) is the cause of determination (adhyavasāya), which is of the nature of certainty;
the mind (manas) is declared to be the seed of volition (saṃkalpa) and conceptualization (vikalpa).
From speech and so forth, as well as from sound and so forth, the hearing of speech and so forth arises;
therefore, the five subtle elements (tanmātra-pañcaka) should be understood as the cause of hearing and the other senses. (28)
The pentad of elements (bhūta-pañcaka) is the cause of light, space, and so forth;
the pentad beginning with Śuddhavidyā consists of the supreme and subordinate powers (parāparā-śakti).
That which is other than that is the supreme power (parā śakti); this is declared to be the reality.
This goddess is the supreme power, containing within her both the pure and impure paths.
When the principles, beginning with earth, have dissolved into their cause,
then the all-pervading Lord emits the subtle elements externally from that very cause alone.
In the supreme will, there is the unfolding (unmeṣa), the bliss, the teaching, and the non-deficiency;
and the existence and the swelling of the powers of action, will, and knowledge—these are the six.
The four letters beyond [the vowels] are said to be of neuter nature; they have ascended into the interior of the power of will (icchā-īśanā) and consist of the manifest and unmanifest worlds.
When the power of will (icchā-śakti) is joined to the consciousness of unsurpassed bliss,
the triangle and then the hexagon arise once the will has attained its firm foundation.
Through the union of the two triangles of the power of unsurpassed bliss, and likewise through the union of unmeṣa, the manifest form of the power of action (kriyāśakti) arises. (35)
The trident, which is the union of the three powers and the devourer of duality, has been described; it proceeds toward its effects through mutual non-opposition.
In no way can this form of theirs be something to be grasped;
for this [form] is the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)—the creative emission (*sarga*)—which is the refinement of the object of knowledge (*vedya*). || 37 ||
The supreme Śakti exists in the form of the sixteen digits (kalās), just as there are fifteen lunar days beginning with the first (pratipad) and ending with the last (amāvāsyā). || 38 ||
Moving within the sun and the moon, they are the causes of their stability;
likewise, they are remembered as the primordial digits (kalās) of creation, whose essence is reflective awareness (vimarśa). 39.
This Goddess Mātṛkā exists in two ways, by way of being both the seed-syllable (bīja) and the womb (yoni);
she is eternally active, having the form of a triangle (śṛṅgāṭa), and is the birthplace of the universe.
The heart is the seed within this [Māyā], which is that supreme light;
just as a tree exists within the seed of a banyan, so too is the entire universe contained herein.
When investigated, this [effect] does not exceed its cause; the reality of jars and the like is nothing other than that of the clay and so forth when analyzed. (42)
Thus speak the final words of the truth-revealing Vedas, because of the certainty that "in the beginning, all this existed as Being alone. (43)

Within this seed-syllable which denotes pure existence, the entire world appears up to the level of Māyā; once the forms of the objective cognitions have vanished, only this [seed-syllable] remains. (44)
Then the Vidyeśvaras and Sadāśivas, whose essence consists of knowledge and action,
dissolve into the trident of Śakti, which is composed of fourteen kalās.
Above and below, within the body of emanation, everything is dissolved;
beyond that, in this way, everything becomes contracted within supreme consciousness. 46.
Or rather, [it is] that which transcends speech and mind, which is stainless wherever it may be,
and whose sphere of experience lies beyond the agitation of the waves of the thirty-six principles.
She dissolves into the Universal Self, whose nature is that of the Great Mantra. || 47 ||
Everything beginning with Śuddhavidyā is contained within Sādākhya by way of the inclusion of the two fortnights.
Or else, the process of dissolution (*layakrama*) consists in the reflective awareness of the intermediate power (*madhyaśakti*).
Whatever other position there may be, if it does not contradict the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is acceptable.
When the abode has been churned by some cause or another, [it becomes] radiant.
By offering all this oblation, one is not afflicted by poverty. || 48 ||
The universe, consisting of five times five and manifested through the fivefold vibration,
he contracts through reflective awareness, becoming solely the universal vibration.
Bringing about the dissolution of this "this-ness" (idam), which is its opposite,
and intent upon his supreme prowess, he enjoys his own nature, which removes all inauspiciousness.
Thus, the great canvas, variegated by the manifestation of the Great Power, unfolds, its body being the universe attached with thirty-six divisions.
Victorious is the supreme, unsurpassed Consciousness, which repeatedly takes the form of vibration.
Reflect, O people: what further manifestation of our own nature remains for us? (51)
Thus ends the *Anuttaraprakāśapañcāśikā*, composed by the venerable Ādinātha.
